subject: ela
title: Theme Signal: Prove What the Story Means
objective: Determine a theme and support it with relevant text evidence and reasoning.

visual.title: Theme evidence signal board
visual.caption: A story map connects a character choice, a consequence, two short evidence cards, and a theme statement.
visual.altText: A story map connects a character choice to a consequence, two labeled evidence cards, and a complete theme statement.
visual.generationPrompt: Create a bold cyber-neon Grade 6 ELA teaching diagram showing a character choice, consequence, two short evidence cards, and a theme statement. Use readable labels, high contrast, no copyrighted characters, and classroom-safe visual metaphors.

teachingSupport.summary: A theme is a message about life, not a one-word topic. Evidence shows what happened, and reasoning explains how it supports the message.
teachingSupport.description: The app turns close reading into a signal hunt: notice a repeated choice or consequence, collect precise evidence, then explain the pattern in a complete sentence.

diagramCallouts.title: Choice
diagramCallouts.body: Name the decision or action the character makes.

diagramCallouts.title: Consequence
diagramCallouts.body: Track what changes because of that decision.

diagramCallouts.title: Theme message
diagramCallouts.body: Write what the pattern suggests about life, people, or choices.

helperNotes: Start with what the character does before naming a theme.
Use two short evidence moments that show the same pattern, not two random quotes.
Add because: the evidence matters only when the reader explains the connection.

commonMisunderstandings.mistake: Writing a topic such as friendship instead of a complete message.
commonMisunderstandings.fix: Finish the sentence: The story suggests that friendship means ___ when ___.

commonMisunderstandings.mistake: Listing a quote without explaining it.
commonMisunderstandings.fix: After the evidence, explain what the character's choice reveals.

commonMisunderstandings.mistake: Choosing a theme that does not match the character's actions.
commonMisunderstandings.fix: Trace the same choice-consequence pattern in at least two places.

teachingSupport.confusionPrompt: Write whether you are stuck on finding the pattern, choosing evidence, turning a topic into a message, or explaining the evidence.

funTasks: Run a theme signal hunt: highlight repeated choices and consequences in a short story.
Build a two-card evidence board and challenge a teammate to find the missing reasoning.
Rewrite a one-word topic into three possible theme messages, then defend the strongest one.

groupHomework.title: Theme signal crew
groupHomework.sharedOutcome: Submit a theme board with a message, two evidence cards, and a because explanation for each card.
groupHomework.parentRole: Ask the student what the character learned or changed, then let the student point to the evidence.

reward: Unlock the Theme Decoder badge after an independent evidence explanation and delayed recall.

evidenceMoves.priorKnowledgeCheck: Ask the learner to describe a character choice and its consequence in a familiar story before introducing theme language.
evidenceMoves.misconceptionCheck: Check for topic-only answers, quote dumping, and evidence that does not match the proposed message.
evidenceMoves.manipulativeRationale: Use choice cards, consequence arrows, and evidence cards so the abstract theme message grows from visible story relationships.
evidenceMoves.problemSolvingStrategy: Trace the pattern, select precise evidence, explain the connection, then test the message against the whole story.
evidenceMoves.workedExample: Model how a character repeatedly avoids asking for help, then show how the consequences support a message about courage and trust.
evidenceMoves.examplesAndNonExamples: Compare a complete theme message with the topic friendship and with a quote that has no explanation.
evidenceMoves.knowledgeConnections: Connect theme to cause and effect, character development, summary, evidence, discussion, and argumentative writing.
evidenceMoves.metacognitivePrompt: Plan the pattern you will trace, monitor whether each evidence card fits, and evaluate whether your message is transferable.
evidenceMoves.interventionTrigger: If the learner gives a topic, mismatched evidence, or no reasoning, route to the corresponding repair path before another quiz.
evidenceMoves.transitionBridge: Theme evidence work prepares learners for literary analysis, claims, commentary, and research writing.
evidenceMoves.feedbackFrame: Name the pattern, point to the first matching evidence card, and ask the learner to complete one because sentence.

sections.warmup: Look at a character choice and predict what consequence might reveal a bigger message.
sections.teach: A theme is a complete message about life. Readers find it by tracing repeated choices and consequences, then explaining evidence.
sections.guidedPractice: Sort story moments into choice, consequence, evidence, and theme-message cards.
sections.independentPractice: Write one theme message, cite two brief evidence moments, and explain how each supports the message.
sections.activity: Build the interactive theme signal board and move evidence cards until the pattern is coherent.
sections.reteach: Return to one choice and one consequence, then complete the sentence: This suggests that ___.
sections.challenge: Test two possible themes against the whole story and explain which one has stronger evidence.

quiz.prompt: Which is a theme rather than a topic?
choices: The story suggests that honest friendship requires difficult conversations
quiz.explanation: A theme is a complete message, not a single topic word.

quiz.prompt: What should you add after a quotation or story detail?
choices: Reasoning that explains how it supports the theme
quiz.explanation: Reasoning connects the evidence to the message.

quiz.prompt: Which evidence best supports a theme about asking for help?
choices: The character refuses help twice, then succeeds after trusting a teammate
quiz.explanation: The repeated choice and changed consequence directly support the theme pattern.

parentTeacherNotes: Use this as the Grade 6 ELA native V3 exemplar. Require a theme message, two relevant evidence cards, and reasoning before awarding mastery.
accessibilityNotes: Provide text and audio versions of the short passage.
Keep evidence cards keyboard sortable and label every connector.
Do not rely on color alone for choice, consequence, or evidence categories.
safetyNotes: Use school-safe, age-appropriate excerpts and avoid collecting student writing beyond the learning record.

learningObjective: Determine a theme and support it with relevant text evidence and reasoning.
successCriteria: I can describe the big idea in Theme Signal: Prove What the Story Means.
I can use a visual model or example to solve a new problem.
I can explain my reasoning and repair a misunderstanding.
I can retrieve and transfer the idea after a delay.
essentialQuestion: How can evidence help us identify the big idea?

knowledge: A theme is a message about life, not a one-word topic. Evidence shows what happened, and reasoning explains how it supports the message.
capability: Determine a theme and support it with relevant text evidence and reasoning.
Use a model, example, or explanation to demonstrate the idea.
reasoning: Use evidence from the model or task to justify a choice.
retention: Retrieve the core idea after the original lesson context is removed.
transfer: Apply the idea to a new example, context, or problem.

phaseModules.title: Notice the challenge
phaseModules.studentAction: Look at the model and describe what you notice about Theme Signal: Prove What the Story Means.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Use a visual model to master Theme Signal: Prove What the Story Means.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can say what I am trying to figure out before I choose an answer.

phaseModules.title: Build a model
phaseModules.studentAction: A theme is a complete message about life. Readers find it by tracing repeated choices and consequences, then explaining evidence.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Choice: Name the decision or action the character makes.
phaseModules.successCheck: My model shows the important parts and how they connect.

phaseModules.title: Spot the parts
phaseModules.studentAction: Sort the examples, evidence, or steps that belong to Theme Signal: Prove What the Story Means.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Consequence: Track what changes because of that decision. Theme message: Write what the pattern suggests about life, people, or choices.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can explain why one choice fits and another choice does not.

phaseModules.title: Try the method
phaseModules.studentAction: Sort story moments into choice, consequence, evidence, and theme-message cards.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Sort story moments into choice, consequence, evidence, and theme-message cards.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can use the model to complete a new example.

phaseModules.title: Explain the why
phaseModules.studentAction: Test two possible themes against the whole story and explain which one has stronger evidence.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Writing a topic such as friendship instead of a complete message.
phaseModules.successCheck: My explanation names evidence or a rule, not only an answer.

phaseModules.title: Show your thinking
phaseModules.studentAction: Write one theme message, cite two brief evidence moments, and explain how each supports the message.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Choose a drawing, spoken explanation, labeled model, or written response.
phaseModules.successCheck: Another learner could understand my reasoning from my proof.

phaseModules.title: Retrieve it later
phaseModules.studentAction: After a short delay, recall the key idea from Theme Signal: Prove What the Story Means without copying the original example.
phaseModules.visualSupport: A theme is a message about life, not a one-word topic. Evidence shows what happened, and reasoning explains how it supports the message.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can retrieve the idea when the order and example change.

phaseModules.title: Use it somewhere new
phaseModules.studentAction: Test two possible themes against the whole story and explain which one has stronger evidence.
phaseModules.visualSupport: A new context, example, or problem that keeps the same underlying idea.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can recognize when this idea is useful outside the original example.

phaseModules.title: Choose your next move
phaseModules.studentAction: Write whether you are stuck on finding the pattern, choosing evidence, turning a topic into a message, or explaining the evidence.
phaseModules.visualSupport: Pick a helper note, alternate model, reteach path, or challenge path based on your evidence.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can name what is still confusing and choose a productive next step.
